title: Luther's barber
hookLine: Luther taught his barber to pray through the Lord's Prayer, Commandments and Creed like a garland

cards: A man who cuts hair for a living asks his customer a question that can be hard to ask out loud: how do you actually pray? The customer is Martin Luther.
The story goes that Luther answered with a little book, written for, in his words, a good friend, Master Peter the barber. In English it's called A Simple Way to Pray.
A well-known reformer, writing a how-to for a man with a razor. Today the path moves from the Anglican prayer book to the Lutheran and Reformed ways, and it starts in a barbershop.

teach.h: A COLD HEART, A LITTLE PSALTER.
teach.b: Luther starts with honesty. He admits there are days his heart is cold and he has no wish to pray.

On those days he takes his little psalter, goes to his room, or to church if people are there, and quietly says the Ten Commandments, the Creed, the Lord's Prayer and some psalms, the way a child would.
Words he already knows by heart. Then he slows down inside them.
He takes one commandment at a time and makes of it a garland of four strands. Instruction: what does this teach me? Thanksgiving: what can I thank God for here?
Confession: where have I fallen short? Prayer: what do I ask? Take the first commandment: "Thou shalt have no other gods before me."
Instruction: God asks to be trusted above everything. Thanks: that God offers to be my God at all. Confession: the other things I lean on harder.
Prayer: help me trust you. Then he turns to Peter's trade.

teach.h: KEEP YOUR MIND ON THE RAZOR.
teach.b: A good barber keeps his whole mind on the razor and the hair. If he chats and looks around, he may cut someone's mouth, or nose, or throat. Prayer needs the whole heart like that.
If, partway through, a thought catches fire, Luther says, let the rest go and listen. In his words, the Holy Spirit himself is preaching, and that sermon is worth far more than our own prayers.
So the method is a trellis, not a cage, there to get a cold heart started, and Luther is glad to see it climbed over.

how: Some Lutherans and other Christians use Luther's method, praying slowly through a commandment, a line of the Creed or a petition of the Lord's Prayer as instruction, thanksgiving, confession and prayer.

o: Master Peter, the barber Luther taught a simple way to pray
a nickname for Luther, who trimmed long prayers down short
the barber who shaved Luther before he faced the emperor

games.q: Luther's simple way — tap the pairs.
p: may cut a nose or a throat
start with the Commandments and Creed

s: Luther said he always felt eager to pray
he admits to days when his heart was cold, and that's when he reached for the Commandments, the Creed and the Lord's Prayer.
Luther turns each commandment into a garland of four strands
Luther told Peter to finish the method no matter what
if a thought catches fire, he says, let the rest go and listen: the Spirit is preaching.

games.q: you're halfway through praying the first commandment, Luther's way, when a thought suddenly lights up in you. what does Luther tell Peter to do?
o: finish the method first; the thought can wait.
let the plan go and listen.
games.why: Luther says to let the rest go and listen, because the Holy Spirit is preaching. the method is there to warm a cold heart, not to fence it in.

practice: Take "Thou shalt not steal," or go back to the first commandment, and give each strand a few breaths: what does it teach, what is there to be thankful for, where have I missed it, what would I ask?
If you pray, speak the four strands to God; if you don't, let the questions turn over quietly. And if one thought takes hold, follow it, the way Luther told Peter to.

wordCard.voice: Luther's barber. Master Peter, for whom Luther wrote a simple way to pray: the Commandments, the Creed and the Lord's Prayer, woven into garlands of four strands.

carryVoice: Your line: a simple way to pray. Four strands, and room for the Spirit. Until tomorrow.
